verses.translation_literal: A song, a psalm, to the sons of Korah.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song, a psalm, sung for the sons of Korah, and offered up in their voices.
verses.directors_commentary: In the Hebrew this heading is verse 1; the KJV prints it as an unnumbered title, which is why its verse numbers run one behind the Hebrew for the whole psalm. The KJV's "for the sons of Korah" picks one meaning of a flexible preposition: the lamed can say the psalm was written for them, belongs to them, or was sung by them. The Korahites were Levite temple singers and gatekeepers, so this is a choir piece for the sanctuary it praises. "Song" (shir) and "psalm" (mizmor, a piece with instrumental accompaniment) are placed side by side, and Ibn Ezra notes that the order of the two words can be reversed with no change of sense.

philological_notes.note: A piece sung to instrumental accompaniment, from the root 'to make music'. Paired with shir, 'song', as a double label for the genre.

verses.translation_literal: Great [is] YHWH and to be praised exceedingly in the city of our God, the mountain of his holiness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Great is the LORD, and worthy of praise beyond measure, here in the city of our God, on the mountain of his holiness.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens with a shout of acclamation, not a prayer, and the actors should treat it that way: this is a crowd in a procession, already inside the place it is praising. The Hebrew has no "is", and the KJV's "greatly to be praised" is faithful; the compact "great and much-praised" is the ancient formula for the greatness of a city's god, the sort of cry Ephesus would later raise for Artemis, here turned on the rival. The final phrase is bare apposition, "the city of our God, the mountain of his holiness", and the KJV's added "in" before "the mountain" smooths it into two places rather than one. City and mountain are the same place seen as civic and as sacred space. Rashi and Meiri take the verse as future (the greatness will be seen when the city is rebuilt); the grammar has no tense marker and the pilgrim-song reading is plainer.

philological_notes.note: A Pual participle: 'one who is praised', 'worthy to be praised'. It is the root of 'hallelujah'. The KJV's 'greatly to be praised' reads the form as a gerundive.

verses.translation_literal: Beautiful of height, joy of all the earth, Mount Zion, the remotest parts of Zaphon, town of a great king.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lovely in her rising, the joy of all the earth: Mount Zion, far in the heights of the north, the city of the great King.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as a pilgrim's first sight of the city, not as a survey report. The verse is a string of titles, each laid beside the last without a verb, and the actors should let them pile up like a crowd arriving.

The KJV's 'Beautiful for situation' is archaic and a little vague. The Hebrew נוֹף is a rare word, and the old commentators already disagreed about it: Rashi offers 'the foliage of a tree' or 'a bride of beauty', Ibn Ezra ties it to 'the district' (cf. Josh 17:11) and dismisses the 'branch' reading, and Radak takes it as a 'region', with a lovely aside that Jerusalem's air is so mild that the sick are healed there. 'Beautiful of height' keeps the sense that the beauty belongs to the mountain's lift. 'Joy of all the earth' is no exaggeration for a pilgrim city: Metzudat Zion says everyone rejoices at the sight of its splendour. The KJV's 'on the sides of the north' reads as a compass direction, but the Hebrew is odder: יַרְכְּתֵי צָפוֹן, 'the remotest parts of Zaphon'. Zion is not geographically north of anything. Meiri reads it as the part of the city that lies north of Jerusalem, citing Isa 14:13, and Metzudat Zion glosses יַרְכָה as 'side', like a thigh at the side of a body. Many modern scholars hear a deliberate echo of Zaphon, the mountain of the storm god Baal in Ugaritic texts, so that the psalm claims for Zion the sacred height that neighbours gave their own god; that is a modern reading, not something the commentaries in the packet say, and it is a live possibility rather than settled. In the same spirit some modern readers hear 'a great king' as a title the Assyrian emperors used; take that as a possibility too. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak think of David, and Radak and Meiri of the Messiah. Note, finally, that the Hebrew has no article: 'a great king', where the KJV capitalises 'the great King'.

philological_notes.note: A rare noun of disputed meaning. Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as 'district, region'; Rashi gives 'the foliage of a tree' or 'bride of beauty'. 'Height' follows the usual lexical gloss; I leave the choice open in the commentary.

'The remotest parts of the north'. Meiri takes it as the northern part of Jerusalem and compares Isa 14:13; Metzudat Zion glosses יַרְכָה as 'side', like the thigh at the side of a person. A further sense, that צָפוֹן is the divine mountain Zaphon of Baal in Ugaritic texts, is modern scholarship; no commentary in the packet says it.

verses.translation_literal: God, in her citadels, has made himself known as a refuge.
verses.translation_dramatic: God himself, within her citadels, has made himself known: a refuge, a high place that cannot be taken.
verses.directors_commentary: Armenot are fortified palace-towers, the strongest part of a walled city, where a king would shut himself up in a siege. The point is a contrast: other cities trust the walls of their citadels, and Jerusalem's citadels are strong because God is inside them. The KJV's "palaces" is not wrong but makes it sound like luxury; the word carries the sense of defence. The verb nodac is a Niphal, "he has made himself known", and the ASV gets this right where the KJV's passive "is known" does not: God is the subject of the revealing. Misgab, "refuge", is literally a "high, unreachable place", a cliff-fort; YLT's "tower" keeps the picture.

philological_notes.note: A high, inaccessible place; a stronghold. The root means 'to be set too high to reach'. A favourite word of the psalms for God as refuge.
Fortified citadels or palace-towers. Metzudat Zion glosses 'palace and sanctuary'.

verses.translation_literal: For behold! the kings assembled themselves; they passed on together.
verses.translation_dramatic: For look: the kings gathered, and they came on together.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm turns from the city to the threat. The little word hinneh, "behold", is a stage direction to the audience: the singer points, and the crowd sees the story in the mind's eye. The "kings" are a coalition, and the line is deliberately unspecific about who they are, which is why later readers could fit it to many invasions, to Gog and Magog (Rashi, Meiri) or the Tarshish fleet (Malbim). Noacadu is a Niphal, "they met by appointment", so this is a planned alliance, not a chance gathering. "Passed on" (avru) is the verb for crossing a border or advancing; the KJV's "passed by" suggests that they merely went past, which misses the menace and fits the next verse's panic less well. The point of the word is that they came all the way up to the city together, and the army's collapse in the next lines is so much the sharper.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of ya'ad: they met by appointment, were convened. The sense is of a summoned, planned assembly.
To cross over, to advance. Rashi reads it as 'to the war'. The KJV's 'passed by' blurs the hostile movement.

verses.translation_literal: They saw; so they were astounded; they were terrified; they were hurried away.
verses.translation_dramatic: They saw. And so they stared, stunned; terror took them; they fled in a rush.
verses.directors_commentary: Four short clauses, each one fewer words than a breath, and the verbs fall like blows: saw, were astounded, were terrified, were driven off. Direct the delivery as the staccato of a collapse. Notice what is missing: the text never says what they saw. The KJV's "they saw it" adds an object, and it seems to refer back to the citadels, but the Hebrew has only "they saw, thus", which leaves the dread unnamed and so greater. Rashi supplies it: they saw God come out and fight. The last two verbs are Niphal passives, "they were terrified, they were hurried", as if something else took the initiative and swept them off. Nehpazu means to flee in alarmed haste, and the KJV's "hasted away" sounds like leisurely hurry.

philological_notes.note: To hurry in alarm, to be rushed away in panic. The passive form suggests that they were driven.

verses.translation_literal: Trembling seized them there, anguish like a woman giving birth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Trembling took hold of them there, in that very place: a pain that doubled them over, like a woman in labour.
verses.directors_commentary: The simile is the heart of the verse. The women's work of childbirth was the ancient world's most familiar image of helpless, unstoppable pain, and the prophets use it again and again of armies that break. The humiliation lies in the comparison: the kings with their warriors are likened to a woman who cannot refuse the pains. The KJV's "fear" for recadah blunts the Hebrew, which is a physical shaking, "trembling", and the KJV and Webster's "travail" is an archaism for labour that most modern readers no longer hear. "There" (sham) is stressed: Radak and Metzudat David both fix it as the spot at the walls of Jerusalem, where they came to kill.

philological_notes.note: Writhing, anguish; the word is used of the pangs of labour. Metzudat Zion glosses it as a convulsion.

verses.translation_literal: With a wind of the east you shatter ships of Tarshish.
verses.translation_dramatic: With the east wind you shatter the ships of Tarshish.
verses.directors_commentary:
A single short line, delivered flat and hard: the sentence has one subject, 'you', and it is God. The crash of the verb is the whole point.

The east wind (קָדִים) is the scorching, violent wind off the desert, the one that dried up crops in Egypt and, in Ezek 27:26, wrecked the ships of Tyre in the heart of the seas. Rashi hears exactly that: it is the wind of judgment, and he cites the east wind that drove back the sea at the Exodus. Tarshish was a far western trading port, and its ships were the largest merchantmen of the age, so to break them is to break the biggest and proudest thing a seaport could send out. The KJV is faithful here ('Thou breakest the ships of Tarshish with an east wind'), though its 'breakest' is archaic. The Hebrew bet is instrumental: God is the one who acts, and the wind is his tool. BBE turns the line into a simile, 'as by an east wind', and there is a respectable ancestor for that: Ibn Ezra and Radak read the verse as comparing the kings' terror in v.7 to ships struck by an east wind. But the Hebrew has no 'like' here, and the dramatic layer follows the Hebrew. The verb is second person, so the actors turn to God; the Targum, by contrast, makes the ships the subject, 'the ships are broken'.

philological_notes.note: The east wind, from the desert; קָדִים also means 'the front, what lies before', and so the east. Rashi calls it a wind of punishment and cites Exod 14:21 and Ezek 27:26.
'Ships of Tarshish' are large sea-going merchant ships, named for a distant western port. Radak says Tarshish was the entry point for ships.

verses.translation_literal: Just as we have heard, so we have seen in the city of YHWH of hosts, in the city of our God; God will establish her unto perpetuity. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Just as we heard, so now we have seen it: in the city of the LORD of hosts, in the city of our God. God will make her stand for ever. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm, the moment the crowd stops describing the enemies and speaks for itself. Let the actors pause on 'so', and let a quiet pride run through the line: what the old stories promised, they have now watched happen. The speech is communal, 'we', and it looks both back to what they heard and forward to what stands.

Note the twofold 'in the city of', the same two words said twice with a different name each time. The first is 'YHWH of hosts' (the KJV's 'LORD of hosts'), the title of the commander of heavenly armies; the second is 'our God', who is also the God of the pilgrims. The repetition builds the ownership: the city belongs both to the great commander and to us. The KJV's 'establish it' is flat. The Hebrew suffix is feminine, 'her', because Hebrew cities are feminine, and the verb is the strong Polel יְכוֹנְנֶהָ, 'make firm, set on foundations'. 'Unto perpetuity' is עַד־עוֹלָם, 'as far as the horizon of time', which the KJV rightly renders 'for ever'. The listeners 'heard' from the prophets, say Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David, and now they see it. Ibn Ezra frames it as speech Israel will utter on their return. Selah is a pause or a musical mark whose exact meaning is unknown; it is left untranslated.

philological_notes.note: A Polel of כון, 'to set firmly, to establish on a base', with a feminine suffix, 'her', for the city. Metzudat David says it means Jerusalem will stand on its base and foundation for ever.
'Hosts', 'armies'. Radak says it means that God is lord of the hosts above and the hosts below.

verses.translation_literal: We have pondered, O God, your covenant loyalty, in the midst of your temple.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the stillness of your temple, O God, we have turned over and over your steadfast love.
verses.directors_commentary: After the noise of the war, quiet. The scene moves inside the sanctuary, and the voice should drop. The verb dimminu is difficult, and the commentators split: Rashi and Metzudat Zion hear "we waited, we hoped" (the sense of dom, "be still"), while Rashi also records Menachem's reading "we thought" (as in Esth 4:13). The English versions all take "we thought" or "we pondered"; the double sense, "we mused, and we waited quietly", is the best way to hold both. The KJV's "lovingkindness" was coined by Coverdale to carry chesed, which is covenant loyalty: the faithful commitment of a party who has bound himself by oath, and not a mood of warmth. The setting in the heichal, the great hall of the Temple that stood before the Holy of Holies, places the thought at the very centre of the sanctuary: worshippers pondering the loyalty that had just saved the city.

philological_notes.note: Piel of damah: to think, compare, imagine; but Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it from dom, 'to be silent, to wait'. Ambiguous, and the ambiguity is probably intended.
Covenant loyalty, faithful love. The older English 'lovingkindness' is a coinage of Coverdale's Bible.

verses.translation_literal: Like your name, O God, so your praise over the ends of the earth; [with] righteousness your right hand is full.
verses.translation_dramatic: As your name is, O God, so is your praise, carried out to the ends of the earth; and your right hand is full to the brim with righteousness.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm now widens from the temple court to the whole world. Let the actors lift their eyes and their voices on 'ends of the earth', then bring the line back down to one image, the raised right hand, heavy and full.

'Name' in the ancient world means reputation and character, not a label, so 'like your name, so your praise' says that God's fame matches what he is. The KJV's 'according to thy name' is fine in sense. The last clause is where English versions drift. The KJV, ASV and BBE all say 'thy right hand is full of righteousness', which is acceptable, but it hides the Hebrew's compact order: צֶדֶק מָלְאָה יְמִינֶךָ, 'righteousness: full is your right hand'. The verb is feminine and agrees with 'right hand' (feminine), not with 'righteousness' (masculine), so the hand is the subject. YLT's 'righteousness hath filled thy right hand' makes צֶדֶק the subject and ignores that agreement. The right hand is the hand of power and of the oath; a hand full of righteousness, rather than force, is the poet's final turn. Metzudat David stresses the contrast: though God has the might, he does not come in a flood of violence, but in righteousness. Meiri takes צֶדֶק as 'justice, uprightness', as in Deut 16:20.

philological_notes.note: 'The ends of the earth', the far edges of the known world, answering 'all the earth' of v.3.

The verb is feminine, so 'right hand' (feminine) is the subject and צֶדֶק is the thing it is full of, not the other way round. Meiri says צֶדֶק here is uprightness, as in Deut 16:20; Metzudat David says power does not come by flood but in righteousness.

verses.translation_literal: Mount Zion will rejoice; the daughters of Judah will be glad, on account of your judgments.
verses.translation_dramatic: Mount Zion rejoices, and the daughters of Judah are glad: because of your judgments, O God, every one of them.
verses.directors_commentary: The KJV's "let Zion rejoice, let the daughters... be glad" turns the verbs into wishes, but the Hebrew imperfects are plain statements: Zion will rejoice, they will be glad. The ASV and KJV chose the jussive for liturgical effect; the Hebrew form does not require it. The "daughters of Judah" are the towns of the countryside, the satellite villages that look to Jerusalem as to a mother city (Rashi cites Num 32:42; Radak explains the same). The picture is of the village women, who traditionally greeted a victory with song and dance, coming up to the mountain. "Judgments" (mishpatim) is a legal word: the verdicts of a judge. BBE's "wise decisions" softens it into prudence; what is celebrated is the sentence executed on the kings. For ancient ears, a God who punishes the guilty is good news for the weak.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'daughters of Judah': the towns that depend on the mother-city. Rashi cites Num 32:42, where the villages are called the 'daughters' of a city.
Your judgments, your verdicts; here the judgment passed on the assembled kings.

verses.translation_literal: Circle Zion and go around her; count her towers.
verses.translation_dramatic: Walk the circuit of Zion. Go all the way around her, slowly, with your eyes lifted. And count her towers, one by one, and do not lose the number.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb has changed. Until now the psalm has told what kings and nations saw and fled; here the speaker turns to the congregation and gives orders in the plural: circle, go around, count. This is a procession, and the actors should play it as one, moving on the beat of the two verbs. Both verbs mean 'to go around' (sabab and naqaf), so Hebrew says the same thing twice with the ring of a march, and the KJV's 'walk about… go round about' keeps that doubling. The KJV is less sure with the third verb: 'tell the towers' is archaic English for 'count', which is exactly what סְפַר means (it is also the root of 'recount' in the next verse, so the count becomes a story).

The commentators disagree about who is speaking to whom. Ibn Ezra reports that these are the words of Jerusalem to the nations, and that some placed them in David's time and others in the days of the Messiah. Radak reads them as an invitation to the nations to see the beauty of the building. Malbim has a darker reading: after the storm that toppled the towers of the other cities, count hers and find none missing. For the actors, the point is the same: a city is proved by walking its wall and checking the towers against the count. A tower was a defensive post and a boast, and a city that could be circled on foot, in an hour or so, was a city that could be seen entire.

philological_notes.note: 'Circle, go around', an imperative plural. It is the same root as the circuit of Jericho's wall in Joshua 6, but this verse does not allude to it; the shared root only means 'to turn about a centre'. Paired with the near-synonym הַקִּיפוּהָ ('go around her'), it makes a processional pair.
'Count'. Rashi glosses it as an expression of number: know how many towers befit her. The same root returns in verse 14 as תְּסַפְּרוּ, 'you may recount', so what is counted becomes what is told.

verses.translation_literal: Set your heart to her rampart; pass through her citadels, so that you may recount [it] to a generation, a later one.
verses.translation_dramatic: Set your heart upon her outer wall. Then climb among her citadels, and look well at them, so that you may tell it, afterward, to a generation that has not yet been born.
verses.directors_commentary:
The procession has reached the wall and goes in. 'Set your heart' is a Hebrew idiom of attention (the heart was the seat of the mind, not of feeling): this is not 'look at' but 'fix your mind on'. The KJV's 'mark ye well' captures that, though the archaism hides the word 'heart', which the Hebrew says plainly (לִבְּכֶם, 'your heart', singular for the plural group, as if one heart were turned). The gloss 'rampart' is exactly right: חֵיל is the low outer wall in front of the high one (Radak, Metzudat Zion, who cite Lamentations 2:8, 'rampart and wall'). The following verb, פַּסְּגוּ, occurs nowhere else; Rashi ties it to פִּסְגָּה, 'summit' (Deut 3:17, 27), so it means to go up to or through the high places, which is why the KJV's mild 'consider' is too weak and the BBE's 'looking well' misses the climb.

The reason is the purpose clause that ends the verse: so that you may recount to a later generation. Nothing in the city is described for its own sake; each wall and tower is evidence for a story that has to be handed on, and the actors should feel the weight of a witness who knows he will be asked to repeat it. 'Palaces' (KJV) is a fair rendering of אַרְמְנוֹת, which can mean any fortified high building or royal residence, and Psalm 48 itself calls God known 'in her citadels' (v. 4), so the audience hears a hint of who is guarding them.

philological_notes.note: 'To her rampart': the low outer wall that stands in front of the high wall. Radak and Metzudat Zion take it so and compare 'rampart and wall' in Lamentations 2:8. The word is easily confused with חַיִל 'strength, army', which a hearer would also catch.

A hapax legomenon. Rashi connects it to פִּסְגָּה, 'summit' (Deut 3:17), and glosses it 'raise up'; Radak says 'see her citadels, which are so high they look like a peak'. The form is an intensive imperative plural.
'Her citadels': the high fortified buildings of a city. In v. 4 of this psalm God is 'known in her citadels as a refuge'; Malbim reads the two verses together.

verses.translation_literal: For this [is] God, our God, forever and ever; he, he will lead us on death.
verses.translation_dramatic: For this is God, our God, for ever and ever. He, he himself, will lead us on, even to the hour of our death.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the song's last line, and it turns from the tour of the walls back to the one who stands behind them. After the order to count the towers and tell the next generation (v. 14), the verse names the reason: "this God", with the demonstrative pointing as a singer would, toward the city just walked through. Then the pronoun is doubled, "he, he will lead us". Hebrew has no need for "he" after a finite verb, so the extra word is emphasis, and the line is aimed against every rival power the neighbouring peoples trusted. Play it quietly, as the confession of a people that has seen the walls and decided where its safety lies.

The last two words are the famous puzzle, and the commentators split. The text here has two words, "al-mut", which Ibn Ezra says the Masorete reads this way, with the sense "until our death", and which Radak also gives first ("until our death he will lead us in this honour"). The other reading takes one word, "almut", as a form of "olam", "forever". Menachem, cited by Rashi, takes it so, and so do Metzudat Zion ("like olamit") and Malbim ("until forever"). Radak then offers it as one word as well, as in "the days of our youth". Rashi's own comment, which is that God leads us as a man leads a small son gently, shows the verb in a tender sense: "nahag" is the verb for driving a flock or leading a child by the hand. The reading you choose changes the last note: either the leading stops at the grave or it never stops. For the stage, I would keep the first, because it is the more human one.

The KJV, "he will be our guide even unto death", is the right sense for the two-word reading. It turns the verb "he will lead us" into a noun, "guide", and it supplies "even", which Hebrew does not have. It is also too soft: "nahag" is an active verb, "he will lead us", with no noun. Note too that the first half of the verse, "for ever and ever", gives the eternal frame, while the second half sets the human frame, our own life. The closing word, whichever reading you take, lands on death or on eternity, and both are heavy.

philological_notes.note: Two words in the text as given: "al" and "mut", with the sense "until death", which Ibn Ezra reports as the Masorete's reading ("until our death"). Radak gives this reading first: "like 'until death', that is, until our death he will lead us in this honour". The other reading takes it as one word, "almut", meaning "forever" (see the next note).

The one-word reading, given by the other commentators: "forever", like "olamit". Menachem, cited by Rashi, takes it so ("he will lead us for ever"), as do Metzudat Zion ("like olamit") and Malbim ("until forever"). Radak adds that it may also be read as one word meaning "like the days of our youth", that is, as he led us in the past, and Ibn Ezra reports a similar view from Rabbi Moshe, from "alum", youth.

From the verb that means to drive a flock or to lead along. Rashi hears in it a father leading his small son gently. The verb is active and finite, "he will lead us", and the KJV's noun "guide" is the translator's choice.
